steps.action:
By the time the foghorn sounded its first warning, Elias had already been awake for hours.

The lighthouse—whitewashed stone, a hundred and twenty steps from base to lantern—sat on a black shoulder of rock that jutted into the North Atlantic like a pointing finger. At low tide, the sea peeled back from the reef to reveal jagged teeth slick with kelp; at high tide, the waves losed themselves in white fury against the cliff, rising, for an instant, taller than the windows of the keeper’s house.

Elias knew every mood of that water. He knew the way it hissed when the wind turned north, the way it boomed and hollowed when a storm was a day away. The night before, lying in the narrow bed beneath the eave, he’d heard a change in the cadence—a deeper note, like a cough under the surface roar. He’d gotten up in the dark, padded barefoot over floorboards polished by his own passing, and opened the door to listen.

Fog, he’d thought. Coming in heavy.

So he had risen early, hours before the horizon bled gray, to polish the lens and check the wick, to walk the narrow balcony and feel the air with his weather-stiff hands. The fog was out there, invisible in the dark, but he could smell it: cold and salt-thick, like a wet stone.

By five, the light’s great Fresnel lens glowed, turning slow and stately, the beam reaching three times a minute across the invisible sea. The building hummed with its mechanism—the soft tic-tic of the escapement, the low thrumming of weight and gear. Elias moved among the familiar sounds as though within the chest of some giant, kindly animal.

Down below, the foghorn bellowed again, a long, mournful sound that went through stone and bone alike. In the keeper’s kitchen, the empty cups rattled in their hooks. On the table, a second plate and mug sat laid out opposite his own, as they had for the past three years.

He poured coffee for himself, then, by habit, for the absent other. The black liquid steamed in the cold air and let go its scent of burnt earth. The second cup remained untouched, a thin skin forming as it cooled.

“Morning,” Elias said quietly, out of old reflex.

There was, of course, no answer.

---

In the town on the mainland, they called him “The Last Keeper,” and always with a touch of disbelief. Most lighthouses these days were automated—a line of knowing lights along the coast, tended by technicians and computers, monitored from distant offices by people whose hands were soft and whose eyes knew more of glass and screen than of sea.

His, though, had been deemed too remote, too subject to strange weather and fickle currents, to be left to machines alone. The maritime board had promised him that it was temporary, an arrangement that would end once they could justify the expense of modernization. That had been eleven years, four ministers, and one dedicated budget line ago.

Elias suspected that they had forgotten him in some back room drawer of public duty—a name written on paper now yellowing, an open folder gathering dust. On calm days, when the gulls wheeled idly and the sea lay flat, the thought would come like a bubble rising from deep within: perhaps they will never come. On storm days, when his world narrowed to light, foghorn, and the shift of dark shapes beyond, he was grateful for their neglect.

He was alone, yes, but not abandoned. The sea never abandoned those who watched it honestly.

---

The fog rolled in with the deliberate certainty of a slow catastrophe. By midmorning, the horizon vanished; by noon, the last rock of the reef was gone. The world beyond the railings dissolved into white. Sounds thickened. The ringing of a buoy’s bell, normally crisp, turned distant and cotton-soft. The faintest slap of wave against stone became close, intimate, as though whispered right beneath the lighthouse’s foundation.

From the lantern room, high above the keeper’s house, Elias watched his own beam cut through the mist: a broad, pale sword that lost its edge five hundred meters from the glass. Within that envelope, the light was absolute, yet beyond it, everything else was swallowed.

He had never liked fog. Storms wore their rage on the surface; you could look at a cloudbank’s green-black underside and know what would come. Fog was a different sort of threat, all silence and concealment. A sea could be flat and gentle while the fog tricked your eyes, turned depth into flat white, sound into the haunt of your own imagining.

Yet ships still moved in it. Cargo schedules and fishing quotas cared nothing for mood or mist.

He checked the radio—nothing new, only the regular reports from the coast guard station and the automated weather bulletins: “Visibility one quarter nautical mile, falling. Wind east-northeast, five knots.” Routine words for anything but a routine day.

At noon, he climbed down the spiral stair to the keeper’s house. The air grew cooler with each turn; stone held the night’s chill well into the day. The steps had worn dips in their centers where his boots had passed thousands of times. He could descend them in the dark, half asleep, and often had.

In the small office just off the kitchen, the logbook lay open. Elias noted the date, the time, the details the regulations demanded: “Fog. Visibility poor. Horn sounding at prescribed interval. Light operational.” His handwriting had become neater with age, the tremor in his left hand forcing his right to move more slowly.

Below that he added his own, unofficial note:

“Sea voice uneasy.”

He’d once stopped making such comments, thinking them fanciful. But one winter, a young inspector from the mainland—a boy with a smartphone always in his hand and hair that the wind could not move—had pointed at an older entry and asked, “What’s that mean?”

Elias had shrugged. “Means the sea sounds different today. There’s something under it.”

And then, only three hours later, they’d received a call: a fishing trawler, taking on water not far off the cape. They had seen her deck lights flickering through the sleet, had watched her ride low and wrong in the waves, had kept the beam on her until the rescue boat arrived.

“That’s just coincidence,” the inspector had insisted, but his smile had been tighter. When he left, he had shaken Elias’s hand with both of his, as though paying silent respect to something he did not believe in but still half-feared.

After that, Elias kept writing what he heard, even if most of the time nothing came of it. To listen, to name, to record—that was part of keeping watch.

---

By late afternoon, the fog thickened into something almost physical. It pressed up against the windows as if trying to peer within. Moisture beaded on the walls of the stairwell and turned the iron handrail slick. The constant, deep moan of the foghorn became the backbone of the day, marking time more surely than the old pendulum clock on the kitchen wall.

The tide was on the rise when he heard it: the faint, uncertain echo of an engine.

He stood very still. For a moment, hethought it might be something imagined, the mind picking patterns from the ever-present wash of sound. Then, again: a low, irregular chug. Not the deep, steady thrum of a cargo ship, not the high whine of the coast guard’s cutter, but something midrange, hesitant.

A small boat, then. Or a fishing vessel.

He went to the radio first.

“This is Raze Head Lightstation,” he said, using the formal call sign though he knew everyone who mattered monitored the channel. “Visibility less than one cable. Sounding foghorn at regular interval. Vessel in vicinity, come in with your position.”

Static answered, crackling with the same impatient energy it always had. After thirty seconds, a voice fizzed through, broken at the edges by distance and interference.

“—Head Light—this is—” The name was lost in a burst of white. “—assist. Chart—malfunction.”

Elias leaned closer, the microphone nearly touching his lips. “Say again, vessel. Give your name, position, and heading. Over.”

More static. A word, half-formed: “—Starling—”

Then nothing.

He tried twice more. No clearer response came. He could raise the coast guard station easily—they were only twenty miles alongshore—but his instinct told him whatever boat was out there was close, closer than anyone else would reach in time.

He climbed, taking the steps two at a time despite the grumble from his knees. At the lantern, he adjusted the rotation slightly, narrowing the sweep. It was a trick that on paper he wasn’t supposed to do; the pattern of the light was set by code and chart, meant to be as unchanging as the rhythm of tide. But there was a little give in the mechanism, and he had old, careful hands. He drew the beam so it lingered a fraction longer on the sector covering the approach to the cape.

The sea beyond remained blank.

He listened instead. Between the horn’s proclamations, he leaned into the silence, the air damp against his face. He filtered out the hiss of fog against glass, the slight high whine of gear and bearing, the soft rattle of something loose down on the balcony. Underneath it, barely there, he caught the engine again.

It came from the north, where the current played tricks even in clear weather. For a second, he pictured the reef as it would look from sea level in this, nothing but white: no rocks, no foam, no horizon. Only the horn and the ghost of light in the mist.

He descended halfway to the watch room, where an old, paint-chipped cabinet held charts, signal flags, and a pair of battered binoculars. The glass fogged when he breathed on it, but it was habit more than hope that made him lift them.

Something moved in the wall of white.

Not light, not shape—merely a thinning, a suggestion. A darker smear within the bright. He held his breath until the room’s small sounds grew thunderous. Then, there: the silhouette of a mast, here and gone between one heartbeat and the next.

He reached for the signal lamp, its metal body cold under his fingers. The shutters clicked as he tested them. He had learned Morse as a boy, had tapped it out with a stick against his brother’s bunk at night long before he ever used it for official messages. By the time electric lamps had replaced old oil-fired beacons, his hands could spell in rhythm without conscious thought.

He aimed into the fog and squeezed the trigger, sending a rapid pattern of short and long flashes: “STOP. HAZARD AHEAD. STEER SOUTH BY EAST. ANSWER IF RECEIVED.”

The beam vanished fifteen meters from the balcony. There was no sense of it touching anything, only the knowledge that light traveled whether or not there were eyes to see it.

For a minute, there was no answer. Then, faint and stuttering, a reply. The lamp on the unseen boat was weak, its intervals uneven, but the message was clear enough.

“INSTRUMENTS FAILING. THOUGHT LIGHT FURTHER OFF. ENGINE TROUBLE. CANNOT HOLD COURSE.”

The letters came broken, but urgency carried between the gaps.

Elias replied without thinking, muscle and tendon remembering what they had done ten thousand times.

“YOU ARE ONE CABLE NORTH OF REEF. TURN TWO POINTS TO STARBOARD, NOW. MAINTAIN. WATCH MY BEAM.”

He adjusted the big lens again, nudging it with the toe of a rag-wrapped boot. The mechanism did not appreciate the interference; it groaned as its perfect ratio of weight and counterweight was disturbed. But the beam swung more deliberately into the dangerous sector and hung there an instant longer each rotation, a white summons in the gray.

Minutes passed, each stretched long. The engine’s note rose and fell, as if whoever helmed the invisible boat worked the throttle in nervous bursts. Elias’s jaw ached. He realized he was clenching it.

Memory intruded, unbidden: another fogbound day, years ago now. Another engine, another uncertain voice on the radio. Back then, he had not been alone up here.

“You worry too much,” Mira had said, leaning one shoulder against the lantern room’s curved glass. “They’ve got sonar and radar and all the other -ars. They use us for romance now, not navigation.”

Her hair, pulled back in a practical knot, had still escaped in wisps that the damp air curled. She had liked bad weather. Storms were something to meet head on, she’d said, like an argument. She’d laughed at fog, at its muffled sulkiness.

They had flashed warnings then, too. They had listened and waited and seen the shape of a trawler loom and then pass, safely distant from the invisible teeth of rock.

“It’s them saving us now,” Mira had said as the boat’s stern light disappeared. “Keeps us from getting too bored.”

The sea had taken her two years later, on a calm day. No romantic storm, no drama—only a misstep on wet rock and a wave that was a fraction larger than the one before. He had not seen it. He’d been inside, making tea. The kettle had still been whistling when he found her.

He shook the memory away, as you shake water from your ears. The sea owed nothing. It took fairly, unjustly, without discrimination. His job was not to hate it or love it, only to watch.

“Come on,” he muttered now, as if to the unseen captain, as if to the fog itself. “Come on, you heard me. Turn.”

As if in answer, the engine’s note shifted. It steadied, climbing to a higher, more confident hum. After another minute, the silhouette appeared again—this time clearly. A small motor-sailer, no more than thirty feet, its mast bare of canvas, its bow cutting cautiously through the mist. It rode higher than it should have if heavily loaded, which at least made it more responsive.

In that first moment, Elias could tell two things: they had turned, but not quite enough; and they were moving faster than safe for this visibility. Panic does that, he thought: makes you think you escape trouble by running harder toward it.

He snapped a new message.

“TURN MORE. MORE. NOW.”

The response came at once, frantic bursts. He did not bother trying to read it. His attention was on the line where the swell broke a little differently—where, beneath the flattening fog, darker shapes waited. He had seen ships that ignored the reef-markers. He had seen their hulls split like overripe fruit, their innards spilling into the surf. He had watched men clinging to rail and rope as waves pounded everything to smaller, quieter pieces.

The bow of the motor-sailer lifted on a swell. For a breath, Elias thought they would clear. Then, as the sea dropped out under them, the low growl of hull against rock reached his ears.

He did not remember moving, but he was already halfway down the stair when the sound came: metal complaining, the higher, thinner shriek of something giving way. His hand slid once on the wet rail; he caught himself against the inner curve of the wall, breath punching out of him.

No time to call the station first. No time to calculate tide or wind. There was water beneath the cliff, then there was not—a drop of twelve meters to the narrow, slick shelf where boats could sometimes tie up on calm days.

He snatched the grab bag that hung by the door—a relic of policies written long before he arrived, containing flares, a length of line, a thermal blanket, a whistle. He added, without thinking, the coil of climbing rope that hung on its own hook and the small, bright orange life ring that had not seen service for three summers.

Outside, the fog swallowed color. The world was reduced to dampness and sound: the horn’s bellow, the slap of waves now edged with a new, uglier tone of impact. The path to the cliff edge was only twenty meters, but the rocks were slick, the lichen treacherous underfoot. He moved with the speed of someone who knew every unevenness intimately but also knew how those familiar contours could betray a hurried man.

At the brink, he lay flat and slid the last half-meter on his stomach, reaching the edge with his head and shoulders before his boots. The drop to the ledge below made his stomach clench even on clear days. Now, with the fog hiding the bottom, it was like looking into absence.

The boat appeared, then vanished, then appeared again in the white, never where he expected it. It had ridden up onto a submerged spur of rock and now ground there with each passing wave. One side of the hull was stove in. A jagged tear opened and closed like a mouth with every lift of the swell.

On the deck, three figures moved as though on someone else’s bad dream. Two adults, one child. The smaller body was swaddled in a bright yellow jacket, the hood too big so it had fallen back, exposing dark hair plastered to a pale face.

The older of the adults—a man, thickset in a navy coat—fought with the liferaft container at the stern. The other, a woman with hair whipped across her eyes, clung to the child and to the rail with equal desperation. The boat’s bow dipped; water burst over it, surging almost to their knees before retreating. With each cycle, the boat wrenched farther from under them, like a rug pulled by an invisible hand.

“You have to get off her!” Elias shouted, though he knew his words would fall apart before they reached. The horn blew; his own voice vanished in it.

He looped one end of the climbing rope around the iron ring sunk into the rock at his feet—a mooring point used rarely in summer, almost never in winter. His fingers slipped once; he cursed and wiped them on his trousers. He checked the knot with the efficiency of long habit, then dropped the coil over the edge.

The line descended into the fog, a fraying umbilical from stone to sea. It fell short of the deck by a meter. He clicked his tongue against his teeth, calculating. The next swell would lift the boat higher; if they timed it, someone could grab the rope.

He made a throwing loop with the spare, testing the weight in his hand. Years ago, he’d practiced this in the quiet months, lobbing coils at the low branch of a skeletal tree behind the cottage. Mira had mocked him then, but she had also taken her own turns, and had been better, in the end, at hitting her target.

“Over their heads, let it fall,” he muttered, as if she were beside him now, as if he were the one being taught.

He waited for the feel of the air, for the rise of the next larger wave. When it came, he threw.

The rope arced in a brief, satisfying curve and came down across the boat’s railing. It smacked wetly against the deck between the two adults. The woman saw it first. Her eyes widened, fixed on the source of the line, trying to find him at the edge of the world.

He thrust
